frozen: 2026-10-26, before any solver or grader run
grading: Score each item 0 or its full points unless the item allows partial credit. Judge substance, not vocabulary: give no credit for naming a framework, a ledger, a field rule or a source of edge unless the answer also does the work the item describes. Arithmetic within the stated tolerance counts. Quote the sentence that earns each point. Apply penalties after summing the items; a case's score cannot fall below 0. Record critical errors separately. Do not use length, confidence or agreement with another answer as evidence.

items.text: Says the gauge carries no directional information: the signed mean (+0.1%, t 0.3) is indistinguishable from zero, so it is not a long entry trigger.
Routes it to sizing, stops, risk limits or option pricing (for example cutting size or widening stops when the gauge is high).
Requires a test of whether the gauge adds anything beyond the coins' own recent realized volatility (or a volatility model of it), not just beyond the unconditional average.
Notes that option or implied-volatility prices may already carry the same forecast, so any option use must compare with implied volatility.
Gives a concrete test design with a rule that would retire or keep the gauge.

critical_errors: Adopts top-decile readings as a long entry trigger.

items.text: Declines to add the score now: its increment on the veto's money gain is nil or negative (+0.31% to +0.30%).
Explains that a signal can be confirmed alone yet add nothing when its information overlaps what the model already uses (rank correlation 0.74 with trailing volatility).
Decides on the money or decision metric, not on AUC (0.802 to 0.806).
Proposes a pre-registered increment test (walk-forward drop-one or add-one with a stated threshold) before any change.
Suggests a cheap check where the score could add value, such as names where distress and volatility disagree, or a different use (sizing, tilt).

critical_errors: Adds the score because its standalone t or the AUC improved.

items.text: Computes per-opportunity expectancy: limit about 0.28 x 2.4% = 0.67% per signal (unfilled at 0) against 1.1% for market entries, so the limit variant is worse (tolerance 0.65-0.70%). Partial 1 point if the comparison is per opportunity but the arithmetic is wrong.
Names the selection: fills happen when price falls, and the unfilled signals are the runners (+4.0%), so per-fill returns overstate the variant.
Proposes a paired forward or shadow comparison on the same signals, scored per opportunity, with a rejection rule.
Does not accept the per-fill +2.4% as evidence of a better policy.

critical_errors: Prefers the limit variant because +2.4% per fill beats +1.1%.

items.text: Deflates for the search: the expected best of 4.2 million independent skill-less trials is about 5.1 standard deviations, so with a 0.45 cross-trial standard deviation the expected maximum annualised Sharpe is about 2.3, close to 2.6; a deflated Sharpe ratio about 0.74-0.76 (below 0.95). Accept SR0 2.2-2.4 and DSR 0.70-0.80, or an equivalent argument that 2.6 is close to what the search alone produces. Partial 1 point for naming the need to deflate without numbers.

Notes that correlated combinations lower the effective trial count and raise the deflated ratio (for example about 0.97 at 10,000 effective trials), so the effective number must be estimated rather than assumed either way.
Removes the midpoint fills: with daily turnover even a few bps of half-spread a day costs several percent a year, and the cost must be measured at the real touch before any Sharpe is quoted.
Notes the negative skew and fat tails widen the uncertainty.
Decides: not deployable now; requires an untouched forward or out-of-sample test with a stated kill rule.

critical_errors: Accepts the vendor's claim that t 6.4 clears the multiple-testing hurdle.

items.text: Recognizes a single pre-registered hypothesis with no free parameters needs no correction for a search that never happened; the live record with real fills is genuine forward evidence.
Approves the increase, or a staged increase toward 2%, with size limits rather than rejecting the strategy.
Checks the remaining risks proportionately: capacity and costs at the larger size, the sample of 46 decisions and its uncertainty, dependence on the central-bank regime.
Gives a monitor and a kill rule for the larger allocation.

penalties.text: Demands a multiple-testing or search correction for trials that did not happen, or rejects the allocation as unproven without a specific flaw.

items.text: Payer: the index trackers, who must trade at the effective-date close regardless of price (a mandate and a clock), so they pay for immediacy.

Mechanism: warehousing inventory and liquidity provision against a known clock, with access because the capacity is too small for large funds; for example buying entrants after announcement and selling into the trackers' close (and the mirror for deletions).

Execution net with numbers: 25 bps spread paid on entry and exit, and capacity sized from $3M daily volume (for example a participation limit per name per day) against the $20M fund; tracker demand estimated from 9% of free float.
Decisive cheap test: an event study on past rebalances from announcement to effective close and after, net of spreads and impact, by period, measuring whether rivals already pre-position.
Kill rule with a number: for example retire if mean net capture over the next N events is below a stated bps level or turns negative.
Payer: farm cooperatives paying a premium to shed drought risk.

Mechanism: warehousing rainfall risk, valuable to this book because drought risk is largely unrelated to its equity exposure, so its reservation price is lower than the hedgers'; sells protection only when the premium exceeds expected payout plus a risk charge.
Bad state and holdability: a regional drought pays out on many contracts at once; sizes the worst season against capital, margin and thin exit liquidity.
Settlement semantics: the named weather station, data revisions, missing readings and threshold definitions decide the payout.
Decisive cheap test: price historical payouts from 30 years of station data against quoted premiums (burn analysis), out of sample, before small live positions.
Kill rule with a number: for example stop if premiums fall below expected payout plus the risk charge, or losses exceed a stated budget.
Recognizes that a minority of trades (8%) carries all the profit, so a +15% target and a tight trail cut exactly the trades that pay.
Says win rate and drawdown are not the decision metric; compares net expectancy and total profit.
Requires an out-of-sample paired comparison against the plain hold on the same signals, with a rejection rule (the 2019-2021 backtest is in-sample).
Offers risk control that keeps the right tail: position sizing, volatility scaling or portfolio limits.
Decides: do not adopt the stop and target as proposed.

critical_errors: Adopts the stop and target because win rate rose and drawdown fell.

items.text: Recognizes that the sleeve's tail is a loss tail (short puts), so capping it is risk control, not cutting a profitable tail.
Prefers the defined-risk long put over the hard stop because a stop can gap through in a crash and fill far worse, and prices the hedge against the premium kept.
Evaluates the bad state with the rest of the book: the puts lose when the long-equity book loses.
Gives a kill or resize rule for the sleeve.

penalties.text: Rejects all protection on the ground that exits or stops cut the right tail that carries the mean.

items.text: Shows the book is close to one bet: with 12 sleeves at average correlation 0.62 the effective number of independent bets is about 12 / (1 + 11 x 0.62) = 1.5 (tolerance 1.4-1.7), or an equivalent quantitative argument.
Judges the thirteenth sleeve by its marginal effect on the portfolio and its stress co-loss, not its standalone Sharpe ratio; a semiconductor sleeve adds to the same technology exposure.
Recommends consolidating overlapping sleeves or capping shared exposure, noting duplicated trading pays costs more than once.
Proposes a decisive measurement: an exposure-overlap map or stress test across sleeves, with a cap or rule.
Decides: do not add the sleeve as proposed.
Flags company concentration: 14 companies supply 62% of events, so the test must count each company once or cluster by company.
Flags era concentration: 70% of events are from 2021, so the effect must be tested year by year and may belong to that period.
Requires a comparison with equally volatile stocks, because volatile stocks often lag and these are three times the median volatility.
Gives a forward or out-of-sample test on new companies and later years with a kill rule.
Decides: not tradeable as a short sleeve yet; counts shorting costs and squeeze risk in any later test.
Recognizes a measured speed edge: a 450 ms lead against a roughly three-second adjustment, confirmed by 60 live releases with real fills (t 4.1), so the public nature of the data does not refute it.
Keeps trading it, with monitors on lead time, capture per release and post-fill markouts as competitors speed up.
Gives a kill rule tied to decay, for example stop when capture net of fees falls below a stated level over a stated number of releases.
Notes capacity is limited to the liquidity inside the adjustment window.

penalties.text: Rejects or winds down the strategy mainly because the report is public and widely watched.
